docs.title: Production ready infrastructure modules for Azure
docs.text:
Graviton CDK is designed to simplify the process of creating and managing cloud infrastructure. It provides a set of reusable components that can be combined to build complex infrastructure stacks.

Warning

The project is currently in alpha stage (v0.x.x), so it is still under active development and may undergo significant changes. Users should be prepared for potential breaking changes as the project evolves.

This documentation is a work in progress and may not be complete.

We expect users to have a general understanding of cloud infrastructure concept and be aware that resources created by Graviton will incur costs in your Azure subscription.

docs.title: Crafted with  by Orbit
docs.text:
Graviton is an open-source project developed and used by Orbit. We are a team of cloud experts with years of experience running production workloads in the enterprise and startup space. docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Primarily focused on infrastructure for application workloads on Azure.
  • Ready to use templated infrastructure stacks for wide range of workloads.
  • Built on top of Pulumi IaC (Infrastructure as Code) framework with Python as the primary language.
  • Based on reusable and composable components with sane and secure defaults from operational best practices and years of experience running production workloads in Azure.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text: Although Graviton is designed to be easy to use, there are a few pre-requisites that you should be aware of before you start using it:

docs.title: General prerequisites
docs.text:
• You should have a general understanding of cloud infrastructure concept and be aware that resources created by Graviton will incur costs in your Azure subscription.
  • Have a general understanding of using Pulumi. Head over to the Pulumi documentation to get started.

docs.title: Software requirements
docs.text:
• Azure CLI installed and authenticated.
  • Python 3.12+ installed.
  • Pulumi CLI installed.

docs.title: Graviton components
docs.text: A Graviton component is a reusable piece of infrastructure that can be used across multiple stacks. Components are defined in the components directory of the Graviton repository.

docs.title: Example components
docs.text:
The following are examples of components that can be used in Graviton:

Component Description az_acr Azure Container Registry az_monitor Log Analytics workspaces, Application Insights & Diagnistic Settings az_network Virtual Networks, Subnets, Network Security Groups & Public IPs

docs.title: Automatic naming
docs.text: The required env, location and workload_name stack configurations are used to automatically generate names for the cloud resources created. Names for resources can often be set explicitly though, especiallyy for services with global uniqueness requirements like Storage Accounts, Key Vaults, Container Registries etc.

docs.title: Naming conventions
docs.text:
In general, we follow the following naming conventions:

{resource_type}-{workload_name}-{env}-{location}-{instance}

For example a resource group might be named rg-myapp-dev-westus-01

Azure best practices

  • Abbreviation recommendations for Azure resources
  • Naming conventions for Azure resources

docs.title: Stacks
docs.text:
Graviton uses Pulumi for provisioning resources. Pulumi uses stacks to configure, group and manage resources in the cloud. Stacks are a way to manage resources as a single unit. Stacks generally consist of services and resources that are related to each other.

Info

For information on stacks in Pulumi, refer to the Pulumi documentation.

docs.title: Configuring stacks in Graviton
docs.text:
Templated stacks in Graviton are called bases. Bases consist of a set of reusable components (usually Azure services).

You may need to set different configurations depending on the configuration schema defined by a base.

docs.title: Example stack configuration
docs.text:
Pulumi stack configuration files are written in YAML. The following is an example of a stack configuration file for a Graviton stack:

Pulumi.prod.yaml
config:
  azure-native:location: northeurope
  azure-native:subscriptionId: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  azure-native:tenantId: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  azuread:tenantId: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  env: prod
  workload_name: myapp

docs.title: Required configurations
docs.text:
• env: The environment in which the stack is deployed (e.g. dev, staging, prod).
  • workload_name: The name of the workload that the stack is deploying.
  • azure-native:location: The Azure region where the resources will be deployed.
  • azure-native:tenantId: The Azure tenant ID.
  • azure-native:subscriptionId: The Azure subscription ID.
  • azuread:tenantId: Entra tenant ID.

Info

Although setting the tenantId and subscriptionId is not strictly required by the Pulumi Azure & Entra providers, we require them to ensure resources are created in the correct Azure subscription and tenant.

docs.title: Optional configurations
docs.text: • resource_group_name: The name of the resource group where the resources will be deployed. If not provided, a new resource group will be created.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Graviton bases use a strict configuration schema to ensure that all required configurations are set. Stacks are configured using Pulumi stack YAML configuration files.

docs.title: Strictly typed and validated configurations
docs.text:
Behind the scenes, Graviton uses Pydantic to validate configurations in a strictly typed manner. Additionally we might use custom validation logic to ensure cloud resources are configured securely.

  • Security: Ensure that cloud resources are configured correctly and in some cases, to prevent accidental misconfigurations.
  • Consistency: Ensure that all resources are configured in a consistent manner.
  • Ease of use: Provide a clear and consistent way to configure resources. Developers can get instant feedback on configuration errors with YAML language servers which support schema validation.
  • Documentation: Configuration schemas are self-documenting and provide information on what configurations are required and optional.

docs.title: Example configuration model
docs.text:
The following is an example of a configuration model for Azure Container Apps HTTP ingress:

class HttpIngressConfig(BaseModel):
    protocol: Literal["http"]
    https_only: bool | None = True

    external: bool | None = False
    target_port: int

    custom_domains: list[CustomDomainConfig] | None = None
    ip_allow_list: list[PrivateIPv4Network | PublicIPv4Network | StrRef] | None = None

    cors: AppCorsConfig | None = None
    sticky_sessions: app.Affinity | None = app.Affinity.NONE
    client_certificate_mode: app.IngressClientCertificateMode = (
        app.IngressClientCertificateMode.IGNORE
    )
